title: Guetteur · active perception with receipts
narration: This is Guetteur, built by Alex Alvord, Cloud Lab Works, Team Drift, for the Open C V AI Competition powered by A W S. It is a depth-vision agent that asks for more evidence before acting, and produces claims you can check. This demonstration uses synthetic depth scenes.

title: OpenCV 5 does the perception work on AWS
narration: The deployed path is a browser dashboard, A P I Gateway, and an ARM sixty-four Lambda running Open C V five. Open C V filters depth, extracts regions, and estimates motion. A deterministic planner can recheck a zone, pause it, compensate for drift, or request approval. The next perception call depends on that evidence. NumPy and Open C V independently remeasure each claim against the same pinned input. The approval selector here is a simulation, not an authenticated remote approval service.

title: Ambiguity changes the next tool call
narration: Here is the live A W S dashboard. We select subtle item removed, the rule planner, and simulated approval. The single-frame evidence is ambiguous. Watch the decision trace: recheck zone requests seven frames. Integrating those frames gives the planner enough evidence to request approval. The trace records the evidence, the action, and the outcome. One approved alert leaves the demo, and both receipt checks pass.

title: Same input · naive baseline misses the change
narration: Now run the same scene and seed through the naive threshold baseline. It does not request the additional evidence. The result is a missed event and a failed task. This comparison tests whether the perception-decision loop changes the outcome, rather than simply explaining a fixed result.

title: No answer means no published alert
narration: Next, a shelf item is removed, but the simulated approval times out. Detection and publication are different outcomes. The system requests approval, records the timeout, and publishes no alert. The score measures detection requests against ground truth; it does not mean an outward alert was sent. The alerts section shows none.

title: A hash is not enough · remeasure the claim
narration: Back on the subtle-removal result, both estimators pass the original claim. Now we deliberately double the claimed depth change. The deployed verifier remeasures the pinned synthetic input. Both checks fail and the altered claim is rejected. Small changes within the documented tolerance can pass. And two estimators over one input cannot establish that the input itself depicts the intended event.

title: Documented failure · below the noise floor
narration: This is the failure case: subthreshold item removed. The change is below the detector's effective noise floor. The dashboard reports a missed event and labels the documented failure. We keep this miss in the results instead of turning it into a success with a different definition.

title: Results, limits, and reproducibility
narration: Across thirty-three synthetic development-set runs, the rule planner succeeds on thirty, compared with twelve for the raw threshold baseline. Event precision is one point zero zero and recall is zero point eight six. The corrected tamper suite rejects twenty-four of twenty-four cases; the initial twenty-three-of-twenty-four result remains documented. Separately, three physical depth-only takes have verified archive integrity and clean shutdown. That is capture evidence, not measured real-world detection accuracy. The M I T repository includes pinned dependencies, tests, deployment instructions, the technical report, and raw results. AI coding assistance and this synthetic narration are disclosed.
